name: The Oberth Effect
statement: A rocket burn buys more energy when fired fast and deep in a gravity well than when slow.
statementAccent: more energy when fired fast and deep in a gravity well
meaning: The Oberth effect is the principle in astronautics that a rocket engine produces a greater increase in a spacecraft's mechanical energy when it fires while the spacecraft is moving fast, deep in a gravity well, than when it fires at low speed. The same amount of propellant, delivering the same change in velocity, yields a larger gain in kinetic energy if the vehicle is already travelling quickly, because kinetic energy grows with the square of speed. The consequence is a maneuver, the Oberth maneuver or powered flyby, in which a spacecraft dives close to a planet or the Sun and fires its engine at the fastest, lowest point of its trajectory, periapsis, to extract the maximum benefit from a given burn. Named after Hermann Oberth, one of the founders of rocketry, who described it, the effect is a key tool for interplanetary and deep-space missions. It can seem to conflict with energy conservation but does not, since the extra energy comes from the propellant.
mechanism: The effect follows from the fact that kinetic energy is proportional to the square of speed. When an engine adds a fixed increment of velocity, the resulting change in kinetic energy depends on how fast the vehicle was already moving, because the energy is the difference between the squares of the final and initial speeds, and that difference is larger when the initial speed is high. Firing when the spacecraft is moving fastest, which in an orbit means at periapsis, deep in the gravity well, therefore converts the burn into the greatest gain in mechanical energy. A complementary way to see it is through the exhaust: when the vehicle is moving quickly, the expelled propellant is left with less residual kinetic energy in the fixed reference frame, so more of the energy released goes into the vehicle rather than into the exhaust. This is why deep-space missions arrange to dive close to a planet or the Sun and burn at closest approach, and why an Oberth maneuver, especially combined with a gravity assist, can produce a far larger change in orbital velocity than the same burn performed slowly far from any body.

examples.text: A spacecraft fires its engine at the fastest, closest point of its orbit around a planet or the Sun to gain the most energy from the burn.
Combining a burn at closest approach with a gravity assist, the Oberth effect adds to the slingshot for a larger velocity change than either alone.
Deep-space missions deliberately fall deep into a gravity well and thrust at the bottom, where speed is greatest, to leave with maximum energy.

variants.name: The Oberth maneuver
variants.text: Falling into a gravity well and firing the engine near periapsis, at maximum speed, to extract the greatest energy gain from a given burn.

variants.name: Powered flyby
variants.text: An Oberth burn performed during a close flyby of a body, often combined with a gravity assist for a larger velocity change.

whyItMatters: The Oberth effect is a powerful tool in spaceflight, letting mission designers wring more useful energy from a given amount of propellant by choosing when to burn. Because propellant is precious and every kilogram must be lifted from Earth, extracting maximum benefit from each burn is central to reaching the outer solar system and beyond, and the Oberth effect shows that timing a burn for the fast, deep part of a trajectory can dramatically increase its payoff. It underlies the design of interplanetary trajectories, escape maneuvers, and especially powered gravity assists, where a burn at closest approach to a planet compounds the slingshot effect. The effect also carries a conceptual lesson about energy and reference frames, illustrating that the work a burn accomplishes depends on the vehicle's speed, and clarifying why it does not violate conservation of energy. As Hermann Oberth's insight from the early days of rocketry, the effect remains essential knowledge for anyone planning efficient journeys through the solar system.

working.lead: Build up speed in a gravity well
working.text: let the spacecraft fall deep toward a planet or the Sun, reaching maximum speed at periapsis.
fire the engine at that fastest point, where a fixed delta-v yields the largest gain in kinetic energy.
depart with a greater increase in mechanical energy than the same burn would give at low speed far from the body.

limits: The Oberth effect is most useful with high-thrust engines that can deliver a large burn quickly near periapsis; low-thrust systems that must fire over long arcs cannot concentrate their burn at the fast point and benefit less. Exploiting it requires a trajectory that brings the spacecraft deep into a gravity well, which is not always available or desirable. The benefit is real but does not create energy from nothing; the extra mechanical energy comes from the propellant, including its own kinetic energy in the moving frame, so the effect is a matter of efficient conversion, not free energy. Its magnitude depends on the depth of the gravity well and the speed achieved. So the Oberth effect reliably increases the payoff of a burn performed fast and deep, within the constraints of engine thrust, trajectory design, and the correct accounting of energy.
misreadings: The Oberth effect does not violate the conservation of energy; the extra mechanical energy the vehicle gains comes from the propellant, whose own kinetic energy in the moving frame is transferred to the craft. It is not that the engine becomes more powerful at speed, but that a fixed velocity change adds more kinetic energy when the vehicle is already fast. And it is not free energy or a perpetual gain, so treating the effect as breaking conservation, or as making the rocket stronger, misreads a principle about how the energy from a burn depends on the speed at which it is delivered.
origin: Named after Hermann Oberth, a founding figure of rocketry, who described the effect in 1927; the greater energy gain from firing a rocket at high speed deep in a gravity well.
